description: We are AstroCadet, a team creating software solutions that connect space science with the next generation. We blend realistic NASA mission simulations with gamified learning through interactive mobile apps, empowering the astronauts of tomorrow to undergo authentic training and explore the cosmos in a fun, engaging way.
summary:
AstroCadet is a 2D pixel-art Mars outpost game for kids ages 7 to 12, built with Flutter. Players command a 4-person crew for 20 Sols (Martian days), spending 3 Action Points per Sol to build, repair, maintain, mine or respond to events while balancing oxygen, energy, water, food, radiation and crew health.

How it addresses the challenge: no choice is free. Solar panels are cheap but dust storms cut their output; the nuclear unit costs more but dust does not affect it. One life-support building of each type cannot supply four astronauts, so players must expand before the Sol 10 communication blackout. Seven events are anchored in real NASA stories: the 2018 Mars dust storm, solar storm radiation at Curiosity, the solar conjunction command pause, and ISS leaks, oxygen generator failures, plant mold and water recycling problems. An in-game Sources screen lists every reference with its link and states clearly that percentages, durations and costs are game values, not NASA data.

Why it matters: kids usually meet space as posters and facts. AstroCadet lets them feel why real missions are hard, and teaches them to ask which numbers are real and which are simplified.
details:
What it does and how it works. AstroCadet is a 2D pixel-art Mars outpost game for kids aged 7 to 12. The player commands a 4-person crew for 20 Sols (Martian days). Each Sol they spend 3 Action Points to build, repair, maintain, mine or respond to events, while balancing oxygen, energy, water, food, radiation and crew health. Seven events (dust storm, solar flare, solar conjunction blackout, life support leak, equipment malfunction, crop contamination, water system strain) test those decisions. The simulation engine is written in pure Dart, separate from the interface, so the rules can be tested on their own.

Benefits and intended impact. Every choice has a cost: solar panels are strong but a dust storm cuts their output, while the nuclear unit gives less power but is not affected by dust. One life-support building of each type cannot supply four astronauts, so players must expand early. Kids learn why real missions are hard, and learn to ask which numbers are real and which are simplified. An in-game Sources screen lists every reference with its link, and states that percentages, durations and costs are game values, not NASA data.

Tools. Flutter and Dart, with the audioplayers, shared_preferences and http packages. Figma for UI design. Spreadsheet and Python simulations to balance the game. NASA sources listed below. Super Intelligence tools (Claude) were used for coding assistance, research and documents; see the SI section.

Creativity. Real NASA events become game mechanics. The “hidden challenge” of the early expansion race teaches a real constraint without any lecture. The game separates real science from game values openly.

Factors our team considered. Keeping systems few and clear for young players, no free choices, honest labeling of invented numbers, replayability through different events, and low barrier to entry.
